title: The perfume (Mark 14:3–9)
hookLine: a woman breaks a jar worth a year's wages over his head and he defends her
carry: she has done a beautiful thing

lines: SHE BREAKS IT OVER HIS HEAD.
cards: A dinner in Bethany, at the house of a man called Simon the leper. Jesus is reclining at the table with friends. Mark has just told us the chief priests and scribes are looking to seize him.
The air is heavy. A woman walks in holding a small alabaster jar of precious spikenard, a costly perfume.

It could have been sold, someone says, for more than three hundred denarii, and in Jesus's own parable of the vineyard, a denarius is a day's pay. She doesn't open it. She breaks it, and pours it out over his head.
The smell fills the room. Nobody can pretend it didn't happen.

teach.b: Some of the guests are furious. Why this waste? It could have been sold, and the money given to the poor.
They scold her. It sounds like a sensible point. But Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Let her alone, why do you molest her? She hath wrought a good work upon me."
The Greek is kalon ergon, and kalon means both good and beautiful; that's why some modern translations say, she has done a beautiful thing.

You'll always have the poor with you, he says, and you can help them whenever you want. It echoes the Law of Moses, which says the poor will not be wanting in the land, and so commands an open hand to them.
But me, he says, you won't always have. She has done what she could.
She's anointed my body ahead of time, for burial. She understood what was coming when the others didn't.

Then a promise: "wheresoever this gospel shall be preached in the whole world, that also which she hath done, shall be told for a memorial of her." And here we are, telling it. Yet Mark never gives her name.
John tells a similar story, also in Bethany, and says it was Mary, the sister of Martha and Lazarus, and that she anointed his feet.

teach.h: SHE HATH WROUGHT A GOOD WORK UPON ME.
teach.b: In Mark, it's his head. And in the scriptures, a prophet anointed a king by pouring oil on his head, as Samuel did for Saul. Messiah means anointed one.
She's the one who does it.

how: Catholics hear the anointing at Bethany in the Passion read on Palm Sunday in the year of Mark, and the Church's anointings with holy oils, at baptism, confirmation and ordination, echo the meaning of the word Christ, the anointed one.

games.q: you're at the dinner. a woman has just broken a jar of costly perfume over Jesus's head. the guests say it's a waste. what does Jesus say?
o: they're right. it should have gone to the poor.
leave her alone. she has done a beautiful thing.
games.why: “Let her alone… She hath wrought a good work upon me.” she's anointed his body ahead of time, for burial.

practice: It's easy to give the sensible amount: the polite gift, the right-sized favor.
Think of one person who has given you more than you ever paid back, and picture breaking the jar for them: your whole evening, a long letter, real attention with the phone in another room.
If you pray, you can offer God something lavish too: time, or thanks.

wordCard.voice: The perfume. A jar broken over his head, a room full of scent, and a woman remembered wherever the story is told. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a good work, a beautiful work. Kalon means both, which is why translations differ.

carryVoice: Your line: she has done a beautiful thing. And she's still remembered. Day fifty-nine, complete.
